scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Wotagei originated from the ōendan cheering squads of the 1970s and 1980s, where fans shouted calls and coordinated movements to support idols.
The practice of MIX calls began around 1993 at idol venues.
The 2002 single "Romantic Ukare Mode" by Miki Fujimoto became emblematic of wotagei, and in 2004, 100 to 200 fans performed it outside Saitama Super Arena, spreading the dance widely.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Wotagei is performed to support Japanese female idol singers during concerts and public appearances.
It also occurs at anime conventions, fan gatherings, and special events like birthday celebrations of idols.
It expresses fan enthusiasm, unity, and artistic support.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Wotagei is performed by wota fans, often holding glow sticks or penlights, called uchishi.

It involves jumping, clapping, arm-waving, chanting slogans, and complex choreographed sequences of named techniques such as thundersnake, rosario, amaterasu, muramasa, romance, OAD (over action dolphin), and PPPH (clap-call rhythm).
Watch for Thundersnake, Rosario, Amaterasu.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Miki Fujimoto is notable for her song 'Romantic Ukare Mode,' closely associated with wotagei.
The group GinyuforcE pioneered cyalume dance and popularized wotagei worldwide, appearing on TV and releasing instructional DVDs.
Wotagei is practiced mainly in Japan but has spread internationally, including Taiwan and North America.
Wotagei descends from 1970s ōendan cheering squads supporting idols, evolving through idol fan culture and the development of choreographed cheering and light-stick dance.
